newsitem.title: INDIA: India farm output could bring down interest rates.
newsitem.headline: India farm output could bring down interest rates.

text.p: Anticipated robust agricultural growth following plentiful monsoon rains may create conditions for India to cut towering interest rates, Planning Minister Yogendra Alagh said on Wednesday.

He told a business seminar in the Indian capital that a slowdown in economic growth stemmed from weak agricultural output in the 1995/96 (Nov-Oct), but conditions were now ripe for higher overall growth.
Food prices rose twice fast as the broader inflation rate last year, discouraging authorities from cutting interest rates to spur economic growth and stoke demand, Alagh told the seminar.
"When food prices were rising, we had no option but to keep interest rates where they are (now)," Alagh said.
But conditions could now be ripe for an interest rate cut, he added.
"I am not saying it will be done. It is not my job. But it may be possible for the monetary authorities to consider a lower rate of interest."

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was scheduled later this month to announce its monetary policy for the six-month period ending next March. It is facing mounting pressure from industrialists to lower interest rates.
The government had previously promised to lower interest rates after containing inflation, which two years ago touched double digits.

However, despite an average annual inflation rate of around five percent over the past six months, the prime lending rates of banks and financial institutions have remained between 16 and 17 percent, among the highest in the world.

This week government statistics revealed that industrial production grew by a provisional 9.9 percent in the first quarter of the current 1996/97 (April-March) fiscal year, against 15.5 percent in the same period last year.
Industries have complained that a shortage of credit, high interest rates and infrastructure bottlenecks caused the slowdown.
Alagh said lower farm output last year could have sparked a slowdown in overall growth.
Grain output had been forecast to be around 190 million tonnes in 1995/96 (November-October), but the projection has been revised downwards to 185 million tonnes, according to industry estimates.
But Alagh said things would be different during the next crop year beginning in November, with farm prices rising at a slower pace.

For the ninth consecutive year, India had normal rains during the July-to-September monsoon season. This week officials said 83 percent of the country's districts received normal to excess monsoon rains this year.
Evenly dispersed monsoon rains were expected to boost farm output over the 1996/97 season starting in November.
